questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is from which author and work?

options.text: John Gall, Systemantics (1975)
Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming (1968)
Doug McIlroy, the Unix philosophy (1978)
Pat Helland, Immutability Changes Everything (2015)

questions.explanation: Gall's law warns that complex systems must be grown from simple working ones — which is what the chapter does: a log is an append-only file, and a stream broker is built from it.

questions.question: What was the one big assumption throughout Chapter 10, and why is it load-bearing?

options.text: That the input is bounded, of a known and finite size
That the input fits into memory on a single machine
That the input has been sorted by key beforehand
That the input is immutable once the job starts

questions.explanation: Chapter 10 read a set of files as input and produced a new set of output files — derived data, meaning a dataset that can be recreated by running the batch process again if necessary, as with search indexes, recommendation systems and analytics.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say a real dataset is never complete?

options.text: Because a lot of real data is unbounded, arriving gradually
Because datasets are always too large to read fully
Because databases delete old data automatically
Because data is always corrupted at the edges

questions.explanation: Artificial chunking is what batch processing does to an unbounded reality.

questions.question: Trace the argument from daily batch to stream processing.

options.text: That changes appear in the output only a day later
Daily batch becomes hourly, then minutely, and stops there
Batch is replaced by request/response processing
Batch is replaced by in-memory databases

questions.explanation: Abandoning fixed time slices entirely is the endpoint of the argument.

questions.question: Give the general definition of 'stream' and where it already appears. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In general a stream refers to data that is incrementally made available over time
It appears in the stdin and stdout of Unix, and in programming languages as lazy lists
It appears in filesystem APIs such as Java's FileInputStream, and in TCP connections
It appears in the chunked transfer encoding used by HTTP responses

questions.explanation: Chunked encoding is not among the examples given. The fourth is delivering audio and video over the internet. The chapter narrows it to event streams as a data management mechanism — the unbounded, incrementally processed counterpart to the batch data of the last chapter.

questions.question: Give the chapter's definition of an event.

options.text: A small, self-contained, immutable object recording something that happened
A mutable record that is updated as circumstances change
A batch of records grouped together by time window
An acknowledgment message sent back by a consumer

questions.explanation: The thing that happened might be an action a user took, such as viewing a page or making a purchase, or it may originate from a machine — such as a periodic measurement from a temperature sensor, or a CPU utilization metric. In the batch-with-Unix-tools example, each line of the web server log is an event.

questions.question: Once an event is encoded, what does that enable?

options.text: Storage, by appending to a file or inserting into a table
Only storage; transmission requires a different encoding
Only transmission; events are never stored
Encoding serves only to compress the event before it is sent

questions.explanation: One encoding serves both persistence and the wire.

questions.question: Give the vocabulary for stream participants and the streaming analogue of a filename.

options.text: Once by a producer, then consumed by multiple consumers
A writer and readers; the analogue is a partition
A leader and followers; the analogue is a log segment
A coordinator and participants; the analogue is a directory

questions.explanation: Analogous to how a file is written once and then potentially read by multiple jobs.

questions.question: Why does the chapter reject using a plain file or database to connect producers and consumers?

options.text: A producer writes to a datastore and consumers poll it
Because a database is unable to store events at all
Because a file cannot be appended to incrementally
Because polling cannot be implemented across a network

questions.explanation: Databases do have triggers, which can react to a change such as a row being inserted into a table, but they are very limited in what they can do and have somewhat been an afterthought in database design — so specialized tools have been developed for delivering event notifications.

questions.question: Define a messaging system and what it adds over a Unix pipe or TCP connection.

options.text: The producer pushes a message that is delivered to consumers
It adds only durability, and not delivery to several consumers
It adds only ordering, and not delivery to several consumers
It adds nothing at all, since a Unix pipe is equivalent

questions.explanation: Many-to-many rather than one-to-one is the structural addition.

questions.question: Which two questions does the chapter say are particularly helpful for distinguishing messaging systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What happens if the producers send messages faster than the consumers can process them?
What happens if nodes crash or temporarily go offline — are any messages lost?
What query language does the messaging system support?
How many partitions may a single topic be split into?

questions.explanation: Within the publish/subscribe model there is no one right answer for all purposes, so these two questions differentiate the systems.

questions.question: Name the three broad options when producers outrun consumers.

options.text: Drop messages, buffer them in a queue, or apply backpressure
Drop the message, retry it, or abort the producer
Buffer, compress, or partition the message stream
Replicate, shard, or cache the pending messages

questions.explanation: If messages are buffered in a queue it is important to understand what happens as that queue grows: does the system crash if the queue no longer fits in memory, or does it write messages to disk — and if so, how does the disk access affect the performance of the messaging system?

questions.question: What does durability cost, and what do you buy by giving it up?

options.text: Writing to disk and replicating, both of which cost performance
Durability is free; giving it up buys nothing
Durability costs storage only, and buys no performance back
Durability costs latency, and giving it up reduces throughput

questions.explanation: Whether message loss is acceptable depends very much on the application: with sensor readings and metrics transmitted periodically, an occasional missing data point is perhaps not important since an updated value will be sent after a short time anyway — but beware that if a large number of messages are dropped, it may not be immediately apparent that the metrics are incorrect. If you are counting events, it is more important that they are delivered reliably, since every lost message means incorrect counters.

questions.question: What strong reliability guarantee does the chapter credit to batch systems?

options.text: Failed tasks are retried and their partial output discarded
That no task in a batch job ever fails in the first place
That output is always written before the input is read
That all output is replicated to three separate machines

questions.explanation: This is the bar the chapter sets for stream processing, which becomes the exactly-once discussion later.

questions.question: Which direct-messaging approaches does the chapter list that work without an intermediary node? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: UDP multicast, widely used in the financial industry for streams such as stock market feeds where low latency is important — although UDP itself is unreliable, application-level protocols can recover lost packets, with the producer remembering packets it has sent so it can retransmit them on demand
Brokerless messaging libraries such as ZeroMQ and nanomsg, which implement publish/subscribe messaging over TCP or IP multicast

StatsD and Brubeck use unreliable UDP messaging for collecting metrics from all machines on the network and monitoring them — note that in the StatsD protocol, counter metrics are only correct if all messages are received, making UDP counters at best approximate
Direct HTTP or RPC requests, as with webhooks, which guarantee delivery because the caller retries indefinitely

questions.explanation: Webhooks do not guarantee delivery — the pattern registers a callback URL with another service, and message loss remains possible. Although these direct messaging systems work well in the situations for which they are designed, they generally require the application code to be aware of the possibility of message loss: the faults they can tolerate are quite limited, since they assume that producers and consumers are constantly online. If a consumer is offline it may miss messages that were sent while it was unreachable, and although some protocols allow the producer to retry failed deliveries, that approach may break down if the producer crashes, losing the buffer of messages that it was supposed to retry.

questions.question: Define a message broker and what centralizing data in it buys.

options.text: A kind of database optimized for handling message streams
A broker is a stateless router with no storage
A broker is a client library, not a server
A broker always applies backpressure rather than queueing

questions.explanation: A consequence of queueing is that consumers are generally asynchronous: when a producer sends a message it normally only waits for the broker to confirm that it has buffered the message, and does not wait for the message to be processed by consumers. The delivery to consumers will happen at some undetermined future point in time — often within a fraction of a second, but sometimes significantly later if there is a queue backlog.

questions.question: Which differences between message brokers and databases does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Retention: databases usually keep data until it is explicitly deleted, whereas most message brokers automatically delete a message when it has been successfully delivered to its consumers — so they are not suitable for long-term data storage

Working set: since brokers quickly delete messages, most of them assume their working set is fairly small, so if the broker needs to buffer a lot of messages — perhaps spilling to disk if they no longer fit in memory — each individual message takes longer to process and overall throughput may degrade

Selection mechanism: databases often support secondary indexes and various ways of searching for data, while brokers often support some way of subscribing to a subset of topics matching some pattern — the mechanisms are different, but both are essentially ways for a client to select the portion of the data that it wants to know about
Staleness and notification: a database query returns a point-in-time snapshot, and brokers behave the same way, offering no notification when new data arrives

questions.explanation: The difference is exactly the opposite: a broker notifies clients when data changes, whereas a database query returns a point-in-time snapshot. Four differences. This traditional view of message brokers is encapsulated in the JMS and AMQP standards, implemented in RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, Qpid, TIBCO Enterprise Message Service, IBM MQ, Azure Service Bus and Google Cloud Pub/Sub — and some brokers can even participate in two-phase commit protocols using XA or JTA, making them quite similar in nature to databases.

questions.question: Define the two patterns for multiple consumers on a topic, and their standard names.

options.text: Load balancing, and fan-out
Load balancing delivers to all consumers; fan-out delivers to one
Both deliver to all consumers, differing only in ordering
Both deliver to one consumer, differing only in selection

questions.explanation: The two patterns can be combined: for example, two separate groups of consumers may each subscribe to a topic such that each group collectively receives all messages, but within each group only one of the nodes receives each message.

questions.question: Why do brokers need acknowledgments, and what problem does redelivery introduce?

options.text: Acknowledgments — the client tells the broker when it is done
Acknowledgments serve only for flow control, and redelivery is impossible
Acknowledgments prevent reordering; redelivery causes loss
Acknowledgments are optional, and they introduce no problems of their own

questions.explanation: A lost acknowledgment on a successfully processed message is exactly the exactly-once problem in miniature.

questions.question: Consumers 1 and 2 share a topic by load balancing. Consumer 2 crashes while processing m3 while consumer 1 is on m4. What order does consumer 1 see?

options.text: m4, then m3, then m5
Consumer 1 processes m3, m4, m5 in order
m3 is lost and consumer 1 processes m4, m5
Consumer 1 processes m5, m4, m3

questions.explanation: Even though the broker otherwise tries to preserve the order of messages — as required by both the JMS and AMQP standards — the combination of load balancing with redelivery inevitably leads to messages being reordered. To avoid this you can use a separate queue per consumer, that is, not use the load balancing feature. Message reordering is not a problem if messages are completely independent of each other, but it can be important if there are causal dependencies between messages.

questions.question: Contrast the transient messaging mindset with the database mindset, and its effect on derived data.

options.text: Because a network request leaves no persistent trace
Both mindsets are permanent; the difference is only in latency
Both mindsets are transient; databases also delete on read
The messaging mindset is permanent and the database mindset transient

questions.explanation: If you add a new consumer to a messaging system, it typically only starts receiving messages sent after the time it was registered; any prior messages are already gone and cannot be recovered. Contrast this with files and databases, where you can add a new client at any time and it can read data written arbitrarily far in the past.

questions.question: What question motivates log-based message brokers?

options.text: Combining the durability of a database with a broker's notifications
Why can we not eliminate the message broker entirely?
Why can we not make all messaging strictly synchronous?
Why can we not simply store messages in a relational table?

questions.explanation: Database durability plus messaging notification is the hybrid.

questions.question: Define a log, and describe how it works as a broker.

options.text: An append-only sequence of records on disk
A log is a searchable index; producers insert and consumers query
A log is a mutable file; producers overwrite the head
A log is an in-memory buffer; producers and consumers share it

questions.explanation: In order to scale to higher throughput than a single disk can offer, the log can be partitioned, with each partition a separate log that can be read and written independently of other partitions — and a topic can then be defined as a group of partitions that all carry messages of the same type.

questions.question: What does the broker assign within each partition, and what ordering guarantee results?

options.text: A monotonically increasing offset within each partition
A global sequence number, giving a total order across the topic
A timestamp, giving order by event time
A hash, giving no ordering

questions.explanation: Per-partition total order, no cross-partition order. Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams and Twitter's DistributedLog are log-based message brokers that work like this; Google Cloud Pub/Sub is architecturally similar but exposes a JMS-style API rather than a log abstraction. These brokers can deliver millions of messages per second by partitioning across multiple machines, and achieve fault tolerance by replicating messages.

questions.question: How does a log broker get fan-out and load balancing?

options.text: Because several consumers can read the log independently
Each approach requires messages to be deleted after delivery
Fan-out requires duplicating the log; load balancing assigns individual messages
Fan-out of this kind cannot be achieved with a log at all

questions.explanation: This coarse-grained load balancing has downsides: the number of nodes sharing the work of consuming a topic can be at most the number of log partitions in that topic, because messages within the same partition are delivered to the same node. And if a single message is slow to process, it holds up the processing of subsequent messages in that partition — a form of head-of-line blocking. A footnote offers workarounds: two consumers could share a partition by each reading a fraction of the messages, for example one reading even-numbered offsets and the other odd-numbered; or you could spread message processing over a thread pool, but that complicates consumer offset management. In general, single-threaded processing of a partition is preferable, and parallelism can be increased by using more partitions.

questions.question: Which broker style suits which workload?

options.text: When messages are expensive to process and need parallelism
Log-based suits expensive messages; JMS/AMQP suits high throughput
Both suit all workloads equally
JMS/AMQP suits ordered workloads; log-based suits unordered ones

questions.explanation: Per-message parallelism versus throughput with ordering.

questions.question: Why can a log broker stop tracking per-message acknowledgments?

options.text: Because messages below the current offset are already processed
Because messages are never lost, so acknowledgments are unnecessary
Because consumers acknowledge in batches of 1,000
Because the broker deletes messages on read

questions.explanation: The consumer offset is in fact very similar to the log sequence number commonly found in single-leader database replication: the broker behaves like a leader database and the consumer like a follower, and the sequence number lets a disconnected follower reconnect and resume without skipping writes.

questions.question: A consumer node in a group dies. What happens, and where do duplicates come from?

options.text: Another node takes over its partitions from its last offset
The partition is left unassigned until the failed node returns
The messages in that partition are lost permanently
The whole consumer group restarts from offset zero

questions.explanation: The gap between processing and offset recording is the duplicate window.

questions.question: How does a log broker avoid running out of disk?

options.text: Old segments are deleted or moved to archive storage
Messages are deleted after acknowledgment, as with JMS brokers
Messages are compressed indefinitely and never deleted
The broker refuses writes when the disk fills

questions.explanation: A disk-backed ring buffer rather than a delete-on-ack queue.

questions.question: Using a 6 TB drive with 150 MB/s sequential write throughput, how long does it take to fill the disk, and what conclusions follow?

options.text: About 11 hours
About 11 minutes, so buffering is negligible
About 11 days, growing with the number of machines
About 1 hour, and the ratio improves with more disks

questions.explanation: 6 TB divided by 150 MB/s is 40,000 seconds, which is about 11 hours. Regardless of how long you retain messages, the throughput of a log remains more or less constant since every message is written to disk anyway — behaviour that contrasts with messaging systems that keep messages in memory by default and only write to disk if the queue grows too large, which are fast when queues are short and become much slower when they start writing to disk, so throughput depends on the amount of history retained.

questions.question: Where does the log-based approach sit in the drop/buffer/backpressure taxonomy?

options.text: Buffering with a large but fixed-size buffer
It applies backpressure to the producers when full
It drops incoming new messages once it is full
It falls outside the three-way taxonomy entirely

questions.explanation: Buffer first, drop the oldest only when the buffer wraps.

questions.question: Which operational advantages does the chapter claim from the log's large buffer? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Time to react: you can monitor how far a consumer is behind the head of the log and raise an alert if it falls behind significantly — and because the buffer is large, there is enough time for a human operator to fix the slow consumer and let it catch up before it starts missing messages
Isolation: if a consumer does fall too far behind and begins missing messages, only that consumer is affected; it does not disrupt the service for other consumers
Safe experimentation: you can experimentally consume a production log for development, testing or debugging purposes, without having to worry much about disrupting production services
Cheap shutdown: when a consumer shuts down it keeps its place in the log by holding a lock on its assigned partition

questions.explanation: No lock is retained — the only thing that remains after shutdown is its consumer offset, which is what makes shutdown cheap. Four advantages, all consequences of read-only, non-destructive consumption.

questions.question: How do offsets make replay possible, and what does that make log-based messaging resemble?

options.text: Reading from a file: a read-only operation with no side effects
Replay requires the producer to send every message again
Replay becomes impossible once the offsets have advanced
Replay closely resembles request/response processing

questions.explanation: Offsets under consumer control are what make a stream reprocessable like a file.

questions.question: What observation opens the door to applying stream ideas to databases?

options.text: That a replication log is a stream of database write events
That a database can be pressed into service as a message broker
That a stream can be stored inside a relational table
That both a log and a database are written to disk

questions.explanation: State machine replication: if every event represents a write to the database, and every replica processes the same events in the same order, then the replicas will all end up in the same final state — processing an event being assumed to be a deterministic operation.

questions.question: Why does a nontrivial application end up with several data systems, and what obligation follows?

options.text: Because no single system satisfies every storage and query need
Because databases are unreliable, so redundancy is needed
Because different teams prefer different products
Because a single system would be too expensive

questions.explanation: With data warehouses this synchronization is usually performed by ETL processes, often by taking a full copy of a database, transforming it, and bulk-loading it into the data warehouse — in other words a batch process. Search indexes, recommendation systems and other derived data systems might be created the same way.

questions.question: Define dual writes, and trace the race in Figure 11-4.

options.text: The application writes to each system explicitly on every change
Dual writes means writing twice to the same system; the race causes duplicate rows
Dual writes means replicating to two replicas; the race causes lost writes
Dual writes means writing synchronously to both; no race is possible

questions.explanation: Unless you have some additional concurrency detection mechanism such as version vectors, you will not even notice that concurrent writes occurred — one value will simply silently overwrite another.

questions.question: What is the second problem with dual writes, and the chapter's diagnosis?

options.text: That one write may succeed while the other fails
That the writes are too slow; the diagnosis is network latency
That the writes use different formats; the diagnosis is encoding
That the writes are unordered; the diagnosis is clock skew

questions.explanation: Two independent leaders with no ordering relationship is the root cause.

questions.question: Why was making the search index a follower historically hard, and what is the name for doing it anyway?

options.text: Because the replication log was treated as an internal detail
Because search indexes cannot accept replication logs; the name is ETL
Because databases forbid it contractually; the name is log shipping
Because replication logs are encrypted; the name is event sourcing

questions.explanation: An undocumented internal log is what made CDC a reverse-engineering exercise.

questions.question: What does CDC do to the topology of your systems, and why is a log-based broker the right transport?

options.text: One database becomes the leader and the others its followers
It makes all systems peers; a JMS broker is the right transport
It makes the search index the leader; any broker will do
It removes leaders entirely; no broker is needed

questions.explanation: Taking data in the order it was written to one database and applying the changes to other systems in the same order means the data in the search index will match the data in the database — and the data stored in the search index and the data warehouse is just another view onto the data in the system of record.

questions.question: Compare the two implementation techniques for CDC.

options.text: Triggers that observe changes and write them to a changelog table
Triggers are robust; log parsing is fragile
Both approaches are equally robust, with no performance difference between them
Only triggers are possible; replication logs cannot be parsed

questions.explanation: LinkedIn's Databus, Facebook's Wormhole and Yahoo!'s Sherpa use this idea at large scale.

questions.question: Match each CDC tool to its source database and mechanism.

options.text: Bottled Water for PostgreSQL, plus Maxwell and Debezium for MySQL
Bottled Water for MySQL, Debezium for PostgreSQL, Mongoriver for Oracle
All four of the named tools work only against PostgreSQL
All four of them use triggers rather than reading the log

questions.explanation: Change data capture is usually asynchronous: the system of record database does not wait for the change to be applied to consumers before committing it. This has the operational advantage that adding a slow consumer does not affect the system of record too much, but the downside that all the issues of replication lag apply.

questions.question: Why can't you always just replay the whole change log?

options.text: Because keeping every change forever costs too much disk
Because the change log is encrypted and cannot be replayed
Because replaying the changes would itself alter them
Because the log carries no ordering information at all

questions.explanation: The snapshot of the database must correspond to a known position or offset in the change log, so that you know at which point to start applying changes after the snapshot has been processed. Some CDC tools integrate this snapshot facility, while others leave it as a manual operation.

questions.question: State the log compaction principle and the role of the tombstone.

options.text: It keeps only the most recent value for each key
Compaction deletes the oldest records regardless of key; tombstones mark them
Compaction merges values by summing them; tombstones are checksums
Compaction keeps the oldest update per key; tombstones mark inserts

questions.explanation: Space proportional to current contents, not to write history.

questions.question: What must the CDC system guarantee for compaction to work, and what does it let you skip?

options.text: Because every update carries the full new value for its key
It must guarantee ordering only; compaction lets you skip the broker
It must guarantee at-most-once delivery; compaction lets you skip acknowledgments
It must guarantee monotonic timestamps; compaction lets you skip the log

questions.explanation: A compacted log is a snapshot, so no separate snapshot is needed.

questions.question: Which databases does the chapter credit with first-class change streams?

options.text: RethinkDB subscriptions, plus Firebase and CouchDB sync
PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle, all with first-class change streams
Cassandra and Riak, via read repair
First-class change streams are not supported by any database

questions.explanation: VoltDB also allows transactions to continuously export data from a database in the form of a stream: the database represents an output stream in the relational data model as a table into which transactions can insert tuples, but which cannot be queried. The stream then consists of the log of tuples that committed transactions have written to this special table, in the order they were committed, and external consumers can asynchronously consume this log.

questions.question: What is Kafka Connect, and what does it enable?

options.text: Kafka Connect
A replication protocol between Kafka clusters
A query language for Kafka topics
A partitioning scheme for Kafka

questions.explanation: CDC tooling plus a durable log gives you a general-purpose integration substrate.

questions.question: Where did event sourcing come from, and why does the chapter discuss it?

options.text: In the domain-driven design community
It came from the Kafka community and is discussed as a Kafka feature
It came from the relational database community
It came from the functional programming community

questions.explanation: DDD origin, streaming relevance.

questions.question: State the biggest difference between CDC and event sourcing.

options.text: CDC captures a mutable database; event sourcing stores the events themselves
CDC works at application level while event sourcing works at database level
They are the same technique described under two different names
CDC records immutable events while event sourcing records mutable state

questions.explanation: Low-level state changes versus application-level facts.

questions.question: What benefits does the chapter claim for event sourcing as a data-modeling technique? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is more meaningful to record the user's actions as immutable events, rather than recording the effect of those actions on a mutable database
It makes it easier to evolve applications over time
It helps with debugging by making it easier to understand after the fact why something happened
It guards against hardware faults by replicating each event to several machines

questions.explanation: Replication is not the claim; event sourcing guards against application bugs, because the events remain available for reprocessing. In the course-enrollment example, the event 'student cancelled their course enrollment' clearly expresses the intent of a single action in a neutral fashion, whereas the side effects — one entry was deleted from the enrollments table, and one cancellation reason was added to the student feedback table — embed a lot of assumptions about the way the data is later going to be used. If a new application feature is introduced, for example 'the place is offered to the next person on the waiting list', the event sourcing approach allows that new side effect to easily be chained off the existing event.

questions.question: Which existing ideas does the chapter say event sourcing resembles, and what about tooling?

options.text: The chronicle data model, and the star schema's fact table
It resembles the relational model, and requires Event Store specifically
It resembles the graph model, and requires Kafka specifically
It resembles nothing previously known, and has no tooling

questions.explanation: Chronicle data model and star-schema fact tables, with tool independence.

questions.question: Why can't you just show users the event log, and what property must the transformation have?

options.text: Because users expect the current state, not the full history
Because event logs are too large; the transformation must be lossy
Because event logs are encrypted; the transformation must decrypt
You can show the event log directly; no transformation is needed

questions.explanation: Determinism is what makes the derived state reproducible.

questions.question: Why does log compaction work for CDC but not for event sourcing?

options.text: Because each CDC event carries the whole new version of the record
Compaction works equally well for both of the two approaches
Compaction works for event sourcing but not for change data capture
Compaction cannot be applied to either of the two approaches

questions.explanation: Replacement semantics versus intent semantics. Applications that use event sourcing typically do have some mechanism for storing snapshots of the current state derived from the log of events, but that is only a performance optimization to speed up reads and recovery from crashes — the intention is that the system is able to store all raw events forever and reprocess the full event log whenever required.

questions.question: Explain the distinction between commands and events, and the moment of transition.

options.text: A command, which may still be rejected
Commands are immutable and events are mutable
Events precede commands, which are their side effects
The two terms are synonyms, so the chapter draws no distinction

questions.explanation: For example, if a user tries to register a particular username, or reserve a seat on an airplane or in a theater, the application needs to check that the username or seat is not already taken. At the moment the command is accepted it becomes a fact — and if the customer later cancels a seat reservation, the fact remains true that they formerly held a reservation for that particular seat, so the change or cancellation is a separate event that is added later.

questions.question: Why must validation be synchronous, and what is the asynchronous alternative?

options.text: Because a consumer cannot reject an event that is already a fact
Validation can be asynchronous, because consumers are free to reject events
Validation takes place inside the log itself as events are appended
Validation is unnecessary altogether when using event sourcing

questions.explanation: Immutability forward means validation must come before the log.

questions.question: How does the chapter resolve the tension between immutable events and changing state?

options.text: That state is always the result of the events that mutated it
That mutable state must be abandoned in favour of logs
That logs must be abandoned in favour of mutable state
That the tension between them cannot be resolved at all

questions.explanation: Examples: your list of currently available seats is the result of the reservations you have processed; the current account balance is the result of the credits and debits on the account; the response time graph for your web server is an aggregation of the individual response times of all web requests that have occurred. Even as things are done and undone, the fact remains true that those events occurred.

questions.question: State the calculus analogy between state and streams.

options.text: Integrating a stream over time, versus differentiating state
State is the derivative of the stream and the stream is the integral of state
Each of the two is the integral of the other, symmetrically
The analogy holds exactly, with no limitations at all

questions.explanation: Integrate events to get state; differentiate state to get a change stream.

questions.question: Reproduce Pat Helland's formulation about logs and databases.

options.text: Because high-speed appends are the only way to change the log
The database is the truth and the log is merely a cache of it
The two are equally authoritative, so either may be trusted
Neither is authoritative; the application code is the truth

questions.explanation: Log compaction is one way of bridging the distinction between log and database state: it retains only the latest version of each record and discards overwritten versions.

questions.question: How have accountants used immutability, and what do they do about mistakes?

options.text: Bookkeeping ledgers, which have been append-only for centuries
Accountants erase incorrect entries and rewrite them
Accountants delete the affected period and recompute
Accountants have always used mutable ledgers

questions.explanation: Compensating transactions rather than erasure — the same discipline event sourcing adopts. Although such auditability is particularly important in financial systems, it is also beneficial for many other systems that are not subject to such strict regulation.

questions.question: A customer adds an item to their cart and then removes it. Who cares?

options.text: That the two events cancel out for fulfillment but not for analytics
Nobody cares, since the two events genuinely cancel out
Only the fulfillment system has any interest in the pair
Only the audit system has any interest in the pair

questions.explanation: Immutability preserves information that mutation discards. As discussed under the philosophy of batch process outputs, recovery from buggy code is much harder if the code is able to destructively overwrite data — but with an append-only log of immutable events it is much easier to diagnose what happened and recover from the problem.

questions.question: Which systems derive read-oriented views from the same event log?

options.text: Druid ingesting from Kafka, and Pistachio using it as a commit log
Only Kafka Streams is able to derive views in this way
Only relational databases are able to derive views this way
No production system actually derives views in this way

questions.explanation: Having an explicit translation step from an event log to a database makes it easier to evolve your application over time: if you want to introduce a new feature that presents your existing data in some new way, you can use the event log to build a separate read-optimized view for the new feature and run it alongside the existing systems without having to modify them. Running old and new systems side by side is often easier than performing a complicated schema migration in an existing system — and once the old system is no longer needed you can simply shut it down and reclaim its resources.

questions.question: Name the idea of separating write form from read form, and its effect on normalization debates.

options.text: Command query responsibility segregation
Event sourcing; it settles the debate in favour of normalization
Materialized views; it settles the debate in favour of denormalization only for warehouses
Schema-on-read; it makes normalization mandatory

questions.explanation: Twitter's home timelines illustrate read-optimized state: a cache of recently written tweets by the people a particular user is following, like a mailbox. They are highly denormalized, since your tweets are duplicated in all of the timelines of the people following you — but the fan-out service keeps this duplicated state in sync with new tweets and new following relationships, which keeps the duplication manageable.

questions.question: What is the biggest downside of event sourcing and CDC, and what are the solutions?

options.text: That consumers are asynchronous, so a reader may not see their own write
That the log grows without bound, and the solution is deletion
That events are mutable, and the solution is adding checksums
That events arrive unordered, and the solution is timestamps

questions.explanation: Reading your own writes is the specific guarantee at risk.

questions.question: How does deriving state from an event log simplify concurrency control?

options.text: That one user action changes data in several places
It requires more multi-object transactions, not fewer
It requires two-phase locking on the log
It has no effect on concurrency control

questions.explanation: A serial order per partition plus co-partitioned state removes the need for locking.

questions.question: To what extent is it feasible to keep an immutable history forever?

options.text: On the amount of churn in the dataset
Always feasible regardless of workload
Never feasible for any workload
Feasible only for read-only workloads

questions.explanation: Various databases internally use immutable data structures or multi-version data to support point-in-time snapshots, and version control systems such as Git, Mercurial and Fossil also rely on immutable data to preserve version history of files.

questions.question: What administrative reasons for deletion does the chapter give, and what do Datomic and Fossil call real deletion?

options.text: Administrative reasons, such as privacy regulations
Only performance reasons; the features are called compaction and vacuum
Only auditing reasons; the features are called redaction and masking
Administrative deletion never arises in practice, so this does not apply

questions.explanation: Truly deleting data is surprisingly hard, since copies can live in many places: storage engines, filesystems and SSDs often write to a new location rather than overwriting in place, and backups are often deliberately immutable to prevent accidental deletion or corruption. Deletion is more a matter of 'making it harder to retrieve the data' than actually 'making it impossible to retrieve the data'.

questions.question: List the three broad options for what you can do with a stream. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Write it to a database, cache, search index, or similar storage system, from where it can then be queried by other clients — the streaming equivalent of keeping derived data systems up to date, and a good way of keeping a database in sync with changes happening in other parts of the system, especially if the stream consumer is the only client writing to the database

Push the events to users in some way, for example by sending email alerts or push notifications, or by streaming the events to a real-time dashboard — in this case a human is the ultimate consumer of the stream
Process one or more input streams to produce one or more output streams, which may consume streams in a pipeline consisting of several such processing stages before eventually ending up at an output
Discard the whole stream once a checksum has been computed

questions.explanation: A piece of code that processes streams like this is known as an operator or a job, closely related to the Unix processes and MapReduce jobs of Chapter 10: a stream processor consumes input streams in a read-only fashion and writes its output to a different location in an append-only fashion.

questions.question: What does the chapter say carries over from batch processing unchanged?

options.text: Partitioning and parallelization
Sorting and sort-merge joins carry over unchanged
Fault tolerance mechanisms carry over unchanged
None of the batch processing machinery carries over to streams

questions.explanation: The one crucial difference to batch jobs is that a stream never ends — which has two consequences: sorting does not make sense with an unbounded dataset, so sort-merge joins cannot be used; and fault-tolerance mechanisms must also change, since with a batch job that has been running for a few minutes a failed task can simply be restarted from the beginning, but with a stream job that has been running for several years, restarting from the beginning after a crash may not be a viable option.

questions.question: Which monitoring applications does the chapter name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fraud detection systems need to determine if the usage patterns of a credit card have unexpectedly changed, and block the card if it is likely to have been stolen
Trading systems need to examine price changes in a financial market and execute trades according to specified rules
Manufacturing systems need to monitor the status of machines in a factory, and quickly identify the problem if there is a malfunction
Weather systems need to aggregate sensor readings and publish forecasts on a fixed daily schedule

questions.explanation: A daily schedule is batch work, not monitoring. The fourth example the chapter gives is military and intelligence systems tracking a potential aggressor. These kinds of applications require quite sophisticated pattern matching and correlations.

questions.question: When was complex event processing developed, and what is the chapter's analogy for it?

options.text: Complex event processing, developed in the 1990s
In the 2010s; the analogy is to SQL joins
In the 1970s; the analogy is to state machines only
In the 2000s; the analogy is to batch processing

questions.explanation: CEP systems often use a high-level declarative query language like SQL, or a graphical user interface, to describe the patterns of events that should be detected. These queries are submitted to a processing engine that consumes the input streams and internally maintains a state machine that performs the required matching, and when a match is found the engine emits a complex event — hence the name — with the details of the event pattern that was detected.

questions.question: How does CEP reverse the normal relationship between queries and data?

options.text: The queries are stored and the data flows past them
CEP stores data long-term and queries transiently, like a database
CEP stores neither queries nor data
CEP stores both persistently, unlike a database

questions.explanation: Persistent queries, transient data. Implementations include Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama, TIBCO StreamBase and SQLstream, and distributed stream processors like Samza are also gaining SQL support for declarative queries on streams.

questions.question: Where does the chapter draw the boundary between CEP and stream analytics?

options.text: Analytics cares about aggregates rather than specific event sequences
The boundary is sharp: CEP is declarative and analytics is imperative
Analytics finds event sequences while CEP computes the aggregates
The two are indistinguishable, so the chapter treats them as one

questions.explanation: In a concrete example you might want to know the average number of queries per second to a service over the last 5 minutes, and their 99th percentile response time during that period: averaging over a few minutes smoothes out irrelevant fluctuations from one second to the next, while still giving you a timely picture of any changes in traffic pattern. The time interval over which you aggregate is known as a window.

questions.question: Which probabilistic algorithms does the chapter name, and what misconception does it correct?

options.text: Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, and percentile estimation algorithms
Bloom filters only, and stream processing is indeed always approximate
HyperLogLog only, and approximation is mandatory
Probabilistic algorithms of this kind are never used in streaming

questions.explanation: Many open source distributed stream processing frameworks are designed with analytics in mind — Apache Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza and Kafka Streams — and hosted services include Google Cloud Dataflow and Azure Stream Analytics.

questions.question: Why is materialized view maintenance a distinct use of stream processing?

options.text: Because maintaining a derived view is exactly what they do
Because it requires a shorter window than analytics
Because it requires no state at all
Because it cannot be done with stream processing

questions.explanation: In principle any stream processor could be used for materialized view maintenance, although the need to maintain events forever runs counter to the assumptions of some analytics-oriented frameworks that mostly operate on windows of a limited duration.

questions.question: How does searching on streams differ from CEP and from a search engine?

options.text: Searching for individual events by a full-text search query
Stream search indexes the documents first, as a search engine does
Stream search is simply another name for complex event processing
Stream search cannot be implemented in practice at any scale

questions.explanation: Stored queries, moving documents.

questions.question: Why don't we normally think of actor frameworks as stream processors? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Actor frameworks are primarily a mechanism for managing concurrency and distributed execution of communicating modules, whereas stream processing is primarily a data management technique
Communication between actors is often ephemeral and one-to-one, whereas event logs are durable and multi-subscriber

Actors can communicate in arbitrary ways, including cyclic request/response patterns, but stream processors are usually set up in acyclic pipelines where every stream is the output of one particular job, and derived from a well-defined set of input streams
Actors are unable to process messages at all, unlike stream operators

questions.explanation: That said, there is some crossover between RPC-like systems and stream processing: Apache Storm has a feature called distributed RPC, which allows user queries to be farmed out to a set of nodes that also process event streams, with those queries interleaved with events from the input streams, and results aggregated and sent back to the user. But note that many such frameworks do not guarantee message delivery in the case of crashes, so the processing is not fault-tolerant unless you implement additional retry logic.

questions.question: Which clock does a batch process use for time breakdowns, and what does that buy it?

options.text: The timestamp embedded in each event
The system clock of the processing machine, for determinism
The broker's clock, for consistency
A logical clock, for causality

questions.explanation: Determinism under replay is the key benefit.

questions.question: Which clock do many stream processing frameworks use for windowing, and when does it break down?

options.text: The local system clock — the processing time
The event timestamp, which breaks down under clock skew
A logical clock, which breaks down at scale
The broker's ingestion time, which never breaks down

questions.explanation: Reasons for processing delay include queueing, network faults, a performance issue leading to contention in the message broker or processor, a restart of the stream consumer, or reprocessing of past events while recovering from a fault or after fixing a bug in the code.

questions.question: Two web requests are handled by servers A and B. What can the stream processor see?

options.text: Two requests handled by two servers with unsynchronized clocks
The processor always sees events in the order they occurred
The processor sees only one of the two events
The processor sees both events with identical timestamps

questions.explanation: Confusing event time and processing time leads to bad data.

questions.question: Reproduce the Star Wars analogy with its years and mapping.

options.text: Episodes IV, V and VI released before I, II and III
Episodes released I through VII in order; the analogy is about sequels
The episode number is processing time and the viewing date is event time
The analogy illustrates windowing rather than ordering

questions.explanation: A footnote thanks Kostas Kloudas from the Flink community for coming up with this analogy.

questions.question: A request-rate stream processor is redeployed and is down for a minute. What does the graph show?

options.text: A backlog processed at once makes the graph spike misleadingly
The graph correctly shows a steady rate throughout the outage
The graph shows a dip during the outage followed by a steady rate
The graph shows nothing at all for the affected period

questions.explanation: A spike that measures the processor's recovery rather than the world's request rate.

questions.question: You are counting requests per minute in event-time windows, and events have shifted to the 38th and 39th minutes. What is the problem?

options.text: When you declare the window closed despite possible stragglers
The windows overlap, so some events are counted twice over
The window counter overflows before it can be reported
No problem arises, since the windows close automatically

questions.explanation: Even a timeout is not safe, because the delayed events may exceed it.

questions.question: What are the two broad options for handling straggler events?

options.text: Ignore the stragglers, and track how many you dropped
Buffer the stragglers indefinitely, or let the process crash
Reorder the whole stream, or discard the affected window
Extend the window forever, or shrink it to zero length

questions.explanation: Drop with metrics, or correct with retraction. In some cases it is possible to use a special message to indicate 'from now on there will be no more messages with a timestamp earlier than t', which consumers can use to trigger windows — but if several producers on different machines are generating events, each with their own minimum timestamp thresholds, the consumers need to keep track of each producer individually, and adding and removing producers is trickier in that case.

questions.question: A mobile app reports usage metrics but is used offline. What happens to its events?

options.text: It buffers events locally while offline and sends them later
The events are lost while offline
The events are sent immediately regardless of connectivity
The events are discarded by the server as too old

questions.explanation: In this context the timestamp on the events should really be the time at which the user interaction occurred, according to the mobile device's local clock — but the clock on a user-controlled device often cannot be trusted, as it may be accidentally or deliberately set to the wrong time. The time at which the event was received by the server, according to the server's clock, is more likely to be accurate since the server is under your control, but less meaningful in terms of describing the user interaction.

questions.question: What three timestamps does the chapter say to log, and how do they correct a wrong device clock?

options.text: Device event time, device send time, and server receive time
Only the device and server timestamps; no correction is possible
Only the server timestamp, which needs no correction
Four timestamps including the broker's

questions.explanation: This problem is not unique to stream processing — batch processing suffers from exactly the same issues of reasoning about time. It is just more noticeable in a streaming context, where we are more aware of the passage of time.

questions.question: Define a tumbling window, with the chapter's example.

options.text: A fixed length, with every event in exactly one window
A tumbling window overlaps with its neighbours
A tumbling window has no fixed length
A tumbling window groups events within an interval of each other

questions.explanation: Fixed length, exactly one window per event.

questions.question: Define a hopping window, with the chapter's example.

options.text: A fixed length, but with overlapping windows for smoothing
A hopping window has no fixed length and groups by inactivity
A hopping window never overlaps with its neighbours
A hopping window is maintained separately per user

questions.explanation: Fixed length with overlap, built from smaller tumbling windows.

questions.question: Define a sliding window, and why fixed-boundary windows would not group its example events.

options.text: All events within some interval of each other
A sliding window has fixed boundaries like a tumbling window
A sliding window is terminated by user inactivity
A sliding window has no length parameter

questions.explanation: No fixed boundaries — relative rather than absolute grouping. Readers most reliably confuse hopping with sliding: hopping windows still have fixed boundaries, whereas sliding windows have none at all and group events that are within the interval of each other.

questions.question: Define a session window and what makes it structurally unlike the others.

options.text: No fixed duration — it groups one user's events by inactivity gap
It has a fixed duration but is allowed to overlap with itself
It groups all users together rather than one window per user
It is identical in every respect to a sliding window

questions.explanation: No fixed duration, per-user, terminated by an inactivity gap.

questions.question: Why are stream joins harder than batch joins, and what three types are there?

options.text: Stream-stream, stream-table and table-table joins
Because streams are sorted; the types are inner, outer and cross
Because streams are bounded; the types are hash, merge and nested loop
Joins are not possible on streams

questions.explanation: Unbounded arrival, three join shapes.

questions.question: Set up the stream-stream join example.

options.text: Detecting trends in searched-for URLs from search and click events
Joining a click stream against a user profile database
Joining two database changelog streams together
Joining a stream with itself by event timestamp

questions.explanation: Both inputs are activity events, joined on session ID.

questions.question: What can go wrong with the timing between search and click? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The click may never come if the user abandons their search

Even if it comes, the time between the search and the click may be highly variable — in many cases it might be a few seconds, but it could be as long as days or weeks, if the user leaves a browser tab open and comes back later
Due to variable network delays, the click event may even arrive before the search event
The chapter suggests joining a click with a search only if the two of them occur within the same minute

questions.explanation: The chapter's suggested window is much wider: join a click with a search if they occur at most one hour apart. Note that embedding the details of the search in the click event is not equivalent to joining the events: doing so would only tell you about the cases where the user clicked a search result, not about the searches where the user did not click any of the results — and to measure search quality you need accurate click-through rates, for which you need both the search events and the click events.

questions.question: Describe the state and algorithm for the stream-stream join.

options.text: State — the events from the last hour, indexed by session ID
The processor queries a database per event and emits matches only
The processor buffers the entire stream history
The processor emits nothing when there is no match

questions.explanation: Two windowed indexes, with expiry emitting the negative case.

questions.question: Describe the stream-table join, and what the process is called.

options.text: Joining activity events with a database of user profiles
It joins two activity event streams within a time window
It joins two database changelog streams together
It joins a single activity stream with itself

questions.explanation: Activity events enriched from a database.

questions.question: How should the per-event database lookup be done?

options.text: Querying a remote database for every single event
Only remote queries are possible for streams
The database must be rewritten as a stream
The lookup must be done in a separate batch job

questions.explanation: The difference from a batch job is that a batch process uses a point-in-time snapshot of the database as input, whereas a stream processor is long-running and the contents of the database are likely to change over time — so the local copy of the database needs to be kept up to date, which can be solved by change data capture: the stream processor subscribes to a changelog of the user profile database as well as the stream of activity events, and when a profile is created or modified it updates its local copy. Thus we obtain a join between two streams: the activity events and the profile updates.

questions.question: How does a stream-table join differ from a stream-stream join in its windows?

options.text: That the table changelog stream keeps the state up to date
Both sides use a finite window of equal size
The stream side uses an infinite window and the table side a finite one
Neither of the two sides needs to maintain a window of state

questions.explanation: Infinite window on the changelog, none on the activity stream.

questions.question: Which events must be processed to maintain Twitter's timeline cache? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When user u sends a new tweet, it is added to the timeline of every user who is following u
When a user deletes a tweet, it is removed from all users' timelines
When user u1 starts following user u2, recent tweets by u2 are added to u1's timeline
When user u1 unfollows user u2, u1's whole timeline is rebuilt from scratch to stay consistent

questions.explanation: A full rebuild is not needed — the tweets by u2 are simply removed from u1's timeline. When a user wants to view their home timeline it is too expensive to iterate over all the people the user is following, find their recent tweets and merge them — so instead there is a timeline cache, a kind of per-user 'inbox' to which tweets are written as they are sent, so that reading the timeline is a single lookup. To implement this cache maintenance in a stream processor you need streams of events for tweets (sending and deleting) and for follow relationships (following and unfollowing), and the process needs to maintain a database containing the set of followers for each user so it knows which timelines need to be updated when a new tweet arrives.

questions.question: What is the timeline process really maintaining?

options.text: A materialized view over a join of tweets and follows
A full-text search index built over all tweets
An aggregation computed over a sliding window
A complex event processing pattern match

questions.explanation: A footnote gives the calculus reading: if you think of a stream as the derivative of a table and a join as a product of two tables u times v, then the stream of changes to the materialized join follows the product rule — the derivative of u times v equals u-prime v plus u v-prime — meaning any change of tweets is joined with the current followers, and any change of followers is joined with the current tweets.

questions.question: What do all three joins have in common, and why does ordering matter?

options.text: Maintaining state from one input and querying it from the other
None of the three requires state, since ordering is irrelevant
All three require global ordering, which the log provides
Only the table-table join requires any state to be kept

questions.explanation: This raises a question: if a user updates their profile, which activity events are joined with the old profile — processed before the profile update — and which are joined with the new profile, processed after? In general form: if state changes over time and you join with some state, what point in time do you use for the join? Another example: if you sell things you need to apply the right tax rate to invoices, which depends on the country or state, the type of product and the date of sale — so when joining sales to a table of tax rates, you probably want to join with the tax rate at the time of the sale, which may be different from the current tax rate if you are reprocessing historical data.

questions.question: What exactly goes wrong when cross-stream ordering is undetermined?

options.text: It becomes nondeterministic, since reordering changes the result
The join fails outright and reports an error
The join silently loses some of the events
The join silently duplicates some of the events

questions.explanation: In data warehouses this issue is known as a slowly changing dimension (SCD), and it is often addressed by using a unique identifier for a particular version of the joined record: for example every time the tax rate changes it is given a new identifier, and the invoice includes the identifier for the tax rate at the time of sale. That makes the join deterministic, but has the consequence that log compaction is not possible, since all versions of the records in the table need to be retained.

questions.question: Match each join description to its type.

options.text: Both inputs being database changelogs
The changelog pair is a stream-stream join and the activity pair is a table-table join
All three descriptions are stream-table joins
The enrichment case is a table-table join

questions.explanation: Both changelogs is table-table, both activity streams is stream-stream, one of each is stream-table.

questions.question: Why is batch fault tolerance easy, and what does it guarantee?

options.text: Restart the task elsewhere and discard the failed output
Batch jobs never fail, so no mechanism is needed
Batch jobs checkpoint continuously like stream jobs
Batch jobs use transactions on HDFS

questions.explanation: It appears as though every input record was processed exactly once — no records are skipped and none are processed twice. Although restarting tasks means that records may in fact be processed multiple times, the visible effect in the output is as if they had only been processed once: this principle is known as exactly-once semantics, although effectively-once would be a more descriptive term, since records genuinely are sometimes processed more than once and only the visible effect is once-only.

questions.question: Why doesn't the batch trick transfer to streams?

options.text: Because a stream is infinite and never finishes
Because a stream process produces no output to hide
Because streams are immutable once they are written
Because streams are already fault-tolerant by construction

questions.explanation: No completion point means no atomic reveal point.

questions.question: Describe microbatching, its typical batch size, and the compromise that sets it.

options.text: Microbatching, as used by Spark Streaming
Microbatching uses batches of one minute, set by network latency
Microbatching uses batches of one millisecond, set by CPU speed
Microbatching has no configurable batch size

questions.explanation: Microbatching also implicitly provides a tumbling window equal to the batch size, based on processing time rather than event timestamps — so any jobs that require larger windows need to explicitly carry over state from one microbatch to the next.

questions.question: Describe Flink's rolling checkpoints.

options.text: Rolling checkpoints written to durable storage, as in Flink
Flink uses microbatching with a fixed one-second window
Flink replicates all state synchronously to three nodes
Flink has no fault tolerance mechanism

questions.explanation: Barriers without a forced window size is the advantage over microbatching.

questions.question: Both approaches give exactly-once semantics only within the framework. What breaks that?

options.text: Once output leaves the processor, it cannot be erased by a restart
Nothing breaks it, since the guarantee extends to every output
Only database writes break it, while messaging remains safe
Only emails break it, while database writes remain safe

questions.explanation: Any externally visible side effect escapes the framework's ability to discard.

questions.question: What must commit atomically for exactly-once processing to appear? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: All outputs and side effects of processing an event take effect if and only if the processing is successful — including any messages sent to downstream operators or external messaging systems, such as email or push notifications
Any database writes
Any changes to operator state
Any acknowledgment of input messages, which must be sent before the database writes so the offset is never lost

questions.explanation: The acknowledgment, including moving the consumer offset forward, must be part of the same atomic commit rather than preceding the writes. In more restricted environments it is possible to implement such an atomic commit facility efficiently: this approach is used in Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB, and there are plans to add similar features to Apache Kafka. Unlike XA, these implementations do not attempt to provide transactions across heterogeneous technologies, but instead keep them internal by managing both state changes and messaging within the stream processing framework — and the transaction protocol's overhead can be amortized by processing several input messages within a single transaction.

questions.question: Define an idempotent operation with the chapter's positive and negative examples.

options.text: One that has the same effect however many times it is performed
An idempotent operation can only be performed once; incrementing qualifies
Both setting and incrementing are idempotent
Neither setting a value nor incrementing one is an idempotent operation

questions.explanation: We want to discard the partial output of any failed tasks so that they can be safely retried without taking effect twice. Distributed transactions are one way of achieving that goal; another way is to rely on idempotence.

questions.question: How can a non-idempotent write be made idempotent?

options.text: Extra metadata, such as Kafka's monotonically increasing offset
By wrapping it in a distributed transaction, which is the only option
By simply retrying the operation until it eventually succeeds
It cannot be made idempotent without changing the database

questions.explanation: An offset stamped alongside the value lets the write detect its own replay.

questions.question: What assumptions does idempotence rest on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That restarting a failed task must replay the same messages in the same order — a log-based message broker does this
That the processing must be deterministic

That no other node may concurrently update the same value. When failing over from one processing node to another, fencing may be required to prevent interference from a node that is thought to be dead but is actually alive
That the target database must support two-phase commit

questions.explanation: Despite all those caveats, idempotent operations can be an effective way of achieving exactly-once semantics with only a small overhead.

questions.question: What kinds of state must survive a failure, and where can it be held?

options.text: Windowed aggregations, and tables used for joins
Only counters need recovery, and only remote state works
No state ever needs recovering in a stream processing job
Only local state works, since remote state is impossible

questions.explanation: Local plus periodic replication, or remote with per-message latency.

questions.question: Match the three frameworks to their state-replication mechanisms.

options.text: Flink snapshots to HDFS; Samza and Kafka Streams replicate the changelog
Flink uses Kafka topics, Samza uses HDFS snapshots, VoltDB uses remote storage
All three of them write HDFS snapshots of operator state
All three of them rely on redundant parallel processing

questions.explanation: Snapshots, compacted changelog topics, and redundant processing respectively.

questions.question: When is it unnecessary to replicate state at all?

options.text: Because state can be rebuilt by replaying the input streams
Never — the state must always be replicated to survive
Only when the operator state happens to be empty
Only when the stream processing job is read-only

questions.explanation: However, all of these trade-offs depend on the performance characteristics of the underlying infrastructure: in some systems network delay may be lower than disk access latency, and network bandwidth may be comparable to disk bandwidth. There is no universally ideal trade-off for all situations, and the merits of local versus remote state may also shift as storage and networking technologies evolve.

questions.question: How does the Summary relate stream processing to Chapter 10?

options.text: Like batch processing, but continuous and on unbounded input
Stream processing is fundamentally unrelated to batch processing
Stream processing replaces filesystems with databases
Stream processing is batch processing with smaller inputs

questions.explanation: Brokers and logs as the streaming filesystem.

questions.question: Give the Summary's definition of the AMQP/JMS-style broker and its appropriate workload.

options.text: The broker assigns individual messages and consumers acknowledge each
The broker assigns whole partitions; appropriate for ordered high-throughput streams
The broker retains all messages; appropriate for derived data systems
The broker drops messages; appropriate for metrics

questions.explanation: Per-message assignment and deletion on acknowledgment, for task queues.

questions.question: Give the Summary's definition of the log-based broker and what it resembles.

options.text: The broker assigns a whole partition to one consumer, in order
It assigns individual messages and deletes them on acknowledgment
It closely resembles a relational database table
It closely resembles a conventional task queue

questions.explanation: Partition assignment, offset checkpointing, and disk retention.

questions.question: Where do streams come from, and what does log compaction add?

options.text: User activity events, sensor readings, and market data feeds
Only from message brokers; compaction reduces retention
Only from databases; compaction removes all history
Only from sensors, since compaction is unrelated to stream sources

questions.explanation: Representing databases as streams opens up powerful opportunities for integrating systems: you can keep derived data systems such as search indexes, caches and analytics systems continually up to date by consuming the log of changes and applying them to the derived system, and you can even build fresh views onto existing data by starting from scratch and consuming the log of changes from the beginning all the way to the present.

questions.question: Which purposes of stream processing does the Summary list, and which time difficulties does it recall?

options.text: Complex event processing, stream analytics, and materialized views
Only analytics and materialized views; the difficulty is clock skew alone
Only pattern matching; the difficulty is ordering alone
Only materialized views; there are no time difficulties

questions.explanation: Three purposes and two time problems.

questions.question: Restate the Summary's fault-tolerance argument and its four mechanisms.

options.text: Because a stream process is long-running and always producing output
Stream jobs discard all of their output on failure, as batch jobs do
Stream jobs are unable to recover from a failure at all
Stream jobs rely solely on replication for fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Finer-grained recovery, via four mechanisms.
